title: Fit an O-ring onto a hydraulic plug: stretch it over the thread by no more than 50%, seat it square and untwisted
instruction: Fit the O-ring into the groove at the base of the plug's thread.
context: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights (about 547,300 US jobs in 2025, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) keep plant hydraulics running, and fitting a new O-ring onto a straight-thread O-ring boss (ORB) fitting or plug is a routine part of hydraulic repair. The ring sits in a groove between the thread and the hex. It is stretched only as far as it takes to pass over the thread, carried down square to the groove and let close into it, then checked seated all the way round. A ring stretched too far takes a permanent set and its thinner section no longer seals. One pushed or rolled down the thread twists. One let go tilted leaves a side on the thread, where it can be cut when the plug is screwed into its port. Here it is the AS568-924 90-durometer FKM ring of a -24 (1.875 inch thread) boss plug.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A blue anodized aluminum bench holder 9 x 9 x 4 cm is fixed to the table, centered at x 34, y -10. Standing hex-down on it on the axis x 34, y -10 is a zinc-plated steel SAE J1926 -24 O-ring boss hex plug: a 2.25 inch (57.15 mm across flats) hex from z 4.0 to 5.4, then the O-ring groove (undercut) 3.6 mm long with a 44.2 mm diameter from z 5.4 to 5.76, its lower wall the hex face, then the 1.875-12 UN thread, 47.6 mm across the crests, from z 5.76 up to the plug's flat end face at z 7.66 with a 1.5 mm chamfer. The O-ring is an AS568-924 bright blue 90-durometer fluorocarbon (FKM) O-ring, 43.7 mm inside diameter with a 3.0 mm section; it lies flat and centered on the plug's end face (z 7.66 to 7.96). Nothing else is on the table; both arms start at their home poses with the grippers open.
scoring: The score is the ring's final condition, after two damage checks. Doing nothing scores 0. Over-stretch: 0, irreversible, if the ring's inside diameter ever passed 65.5 mm, 50% stretch. Machinery's Handbook advises against stretching an O-ring's inside diameter more than 50% to install it, since a ring stretched further takes a permanent set and no longer fills its groove. In the sim the stretch is the loop round one gripper's two fingertips (and the thread once both are outside it), which reaches 50% at a 73.7 mm pad gap. A real trial measures it the same way: the gripper's logged opening over 73.7 mm while the ring is round the thread (80.9 mm while it is still above the end face) scores 0. That log is the main measure, since it catches a brief stretch the ring may not keep. A two-hand stretch is outside the sim's model; a real trial reads it from both arms' logged fingertip positions or the cone. The secondary check is the ring itself: rolled off after the trial, it is dropped on a sizing cone marked in 0.5 mm diameters beside an unused ring from the same bag; one that settles at a larger diameter has taken a set. Twist: 0 if the ring is left with more than 90 degrees of roll. A ring pushed down the thread instead of stretched over it rolls, 38 degrees per mm for its 3.0 mm section, and after a quarter turn (2.4 mm) its mold parting line has moved from its outside onto its face. A twisted ring can spiral in the groove and leak, so a fitter replaces it. The sim models the roll; a real trial checks the parting line by eye and on the top photo. 1.0: seated, in the groove all round (so square, with no side on the thread), closed onto its 44.2 mm bottom, untwisted (90 degrees of roll or less), with no fingertip left in it, since a ring held open on the fingers has not closed into the groove, and no gripper touching it. Only the ring as it ends is judged, however it got there: let go square, stretched again and let go square, or pressed down. 0.75: seated just as for 1.0, but a gripper still touches the ring at the end. In the sim that is contact, not nearness: the gripper's own shape (palm, fingers and pads at their present opening) within 2 mm of the ring, the solver's resting gap plus the fit of the shapes to the gripper's meshes. The fit is right but not handed off, since a hand still on the ring can still roll it out of the groove, so it is worth less than a ring let go and left alone, and more than a ring at the groove that is not yet seated (0.5). A real trial checks the last top and wrist camera frames for any part of the gripper resting on the ring. 0.5: at the groove (its middle within the 3.6 mm groove) but still on the fingertips or with one side on the thread. That ring is undamaged and only needs closing or pushing square, so it is half the job. In the sim a ring let go more than 4 degrees off square lands that way: across its 50 mm the tilt lifts the far side 3.5 mm, more than its 3.0 mm section, so that side closes onto the thread just above the groove. As a fitter does, a fingertip pressing that high side down 1.5 mm (half its section) pushes it over the last crest, and the ring's own tension pulls it into the groove. The press rolls it 57 degrees (1.5 mm), under the 90-degree limit, so a ring fixed that way is seated and scores 1.0. This press law is a stand-in for a real press, so a real trial scores the ring that results, not the press. A real trial checks the final ring on the top photo (visible in the groove all round, parting line straight) and by a fingertip run round it. 0.25: stretched over the thread and, at the end, still at least 5 mm down it, not at the groove (where it is then, not the deepest it reached). Its middle is then 3.5 mm past the 1.5 mm chamfer, over more than a full 2.1 mm thread pitch, so it is clearly started, undamaged, a quarter of the job; a real trial reads it against the mm scale on the holder. Else 0. Where the arms end is not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Roll the ring out of the groove with a plastic O-ring pick (never a metal one), check it on the sizing cone against an unused ring from the same bag and its parting line straight, and replace it if not (rings are cheap and over-stretched ones are scrapped). Lay it flat and centered on the plug's end face.
fidelity: The ring has no contact simulation: its place along the plug, stretch and twist are a model driven by one gripper's two fingertips (a two-hand stretch is not modeled). It is tied to the plug's axis, a stand-in for fingertips keeping it centered, and a 1.5 mm fingertip press on a cocked side seats it by a rule standing in for a real press. A real trial reads stretch from the logged pad gap (a sizing cone second) and checks the top photo: the ring in the groove all round, parting line untwisted.
